The scale · try it

How a level is decided

Every judge follows one mapping rule. A bright line named in the rubric forces a 0 and overrides everything; otherwise all checks passing is a 1.0, and anything else is a 0.5. Toggle the checks below to watch it resolve.

Calibration · 660 real samples

Score it yourself

The same exercise the validation protocol asks you to run on a judge, run on you. A sample is drawn from the labelled test sets with its label hidden; you pick a level, and the rubric's reasoning is revealed. The number that matters is the bottom row — how often you cry hard failure where the label is not 0, and how often you miss one.

Corpus · browse

The labelled test sets

660 samples — 60 per judge, 20 at each level. Model-written and model-labelled, then scored blind by an independent verifier. Where the two disagreed the row is marked contested; those 68 are the first items an SME should adjudicate, because two capable models splitting on the same rubric usually means the rubric is ambiguous at that point.

Rubric text is the artifact under change control — a comma in a rubric is a code change. Everything here is generated from judges/ and data/testsets/; the static readme is README.html and the reasoning is in docs/whitepaper.md.

Status: proposed, not validated. No judge here has scored a real transcript, and no agreement figure exists for any of them.
